lines: Every guide to running AI agents says the same thing at the end.
Keep a human in the loop.
And not one of them tells you what that human is supposed to be looking at.
chapter: What the human is supposed to look at

lines: Because the obvious answer, reading everything the agents produce, is the one thing that cannot work.
You built the team so you wouldn't have to read every version of the work.
If you read every version anyway, you've hired three agents to give yourself a second job.
So this video is the other answer.
Four alarms.
Four conditions that cannot be true if your agent team is working, each one checked automatically on every run, each one wired to somewhere you'll actually see it.
Set them up once, and you can stop watching.
Start with why reading the output doesn't work, even when you have the time.
In the thirty day experiment, three of the five failures produced output that looked completely normal.
A page with five items on it.
A list with a reason next to every entry.
Nothing about any of it said broken.
That's the pattern with agents.
They don't fail loudly.
A crashed script throws an error.
A confused agent writes you something fluent and plausible, and fluent and plausible is exactly what working output looks like too.
So you stop asking whether the output is good, which needs judgment, and start asking whether the output has the right shape, which a few lines of code can answer every single time.
An alarm is a condition that cannot be true if everything is working.
If it is true, something is wrong, even when every page looks fine.
Alarm one, the run that produced nothing.
The first alarm is the simplest and it catches the most.
chapter: Alarm 1: the run that produced nothing

lines: Every scheduled run should end with something delivered.
A page published, a message posted, a file saved.
So count it.
If a run finishes and the count is zero, that's an alarm.
And the important part is what counts as zero.
A run that errored is zero.
A run that found nothing worth reporting is zero, unless you've decided that an empty week is a valid result and it says so.
And a run that's sitting in an approval queue waiting for a click is zero, which is the one that catches people, because nothing failed.
That last case is why this alarm has to check the queue, not just the logs.
A request that has waited more than a day is a run that produced nothing, it just hasn't admitted it yet.

pills: Check the queue, not just the logs

lines: Alarm two, the step that never says no.
The second alarm watches any agent whose job is to filter.
chapter: Alarm 2: the step that never says no

lines: A judgment step, a reviewer, a triage agent.
Anything that's supposed to throw some of its input away.

pills: Its job is to throw things away

lines: Count what goes in and what comes out.
If it passes through everything, every run, it isn't filtering, it's formatting.
In the thirty day experiment the judgment agent marked every single item as worth covering for three weeks straight, and the output looked thoughtful the whole time.
So the alarm is a pass-through rate.
If a filtering step keeps a hundred percent of its input three runs in a row, tell me.
You'll want to tune the number to your own work, but the principle doesn't change.

pills: 100% kept, three runs in a row

lines: A filter that never removes anything is broken, however good its reasons sound.

blocks.html: A filter that never removes anything

lines: Alarm three, the missing field.
The third alarm checks the contract.
Every agent team has a few things that have to be on every item it produces.
For a research page that's a source link and a date.
For an email triage agent it might be the sender and a suggested action.
Write that list down, and then check it in code, not in the prompt.
A prompt that says always include a source is a request.
A check that rejects any item without a link is a guarantee.
Information drops out at handoffs between agents, quietly, and this is the alarm that notices.
When it fires, it should say which item and which field, so you can see straight away whether one agent dropped it or the source never had it.
Alarm four, the bill.
The fourth alarm is about money, and it's the one people set up last and wish they'd set up first.
Put a ceiling on what a single run is allowed to spend, and alert at half of it.
Not at the ceiling, at half, because by the time you hit the ceiling the run has already cost you the money.
Then track one more number, which is cost per useful output.
Not cost per run, cost per page you'd actually send.
A team that gets cheaper per run but produces fewer usable pages is getting more expensive, and only that second number shows it.
That's the four.
A run that produced nothing.
A filter that never says no.
A required field that's missing.
A run that costs more than it should.
Now where they live.
The checks themselves are deliberately boring.
A final step at the end of each run, or a small script that reads what the run produced.
Don't use your most expensive model to check your other models.
Counting and comparing is exactly the work code is for.
Where the alarms go matters more than how they're built.
An alarm in a dashboard you don't open is the same as no alarm.
Send them to your phone or to a channel you already have open all day.
And write each one as one plain sentence, like, the Monday run produced nothing and has been waiting for approval for thirty hours.
Then test every alarm by breaking it on purpose.
Turn off a tool, delete a link, set the spending cap low, and make sure the right sentence arrives where you'll see it.
An alarm you've never seen fire is an alarm you're only hoping works.
There's one way this goes wrong, and it's too many alarms.
If one of them fires every week for something that turns out to be fine, within a month you'll stop reading it, and then you're back to no alarms at all.
So tune them until they're quiet.
When an alarm fires and nothing was wrong, change the threshold or change the rule that same day.
The goal is an alarm that stays silent for weeks, so that when it does speak, you stop what you're doing.

blocks.html: Wrong alarm? Fix the rule the same day.
Silent for weeks. Then it matters.

lines: And to be clear about what these don't do.
Alarms catch the shape of a failure, not the quality of the work.
A page can have five items, all sourced, all dated, under budget, and still be about the wrong things.
So keep one small habit.
Once a week, read one output end to end.
Not all of them, one.
Five minutes.
The alarms cover everything that can be counted, and that one read covers the rest.

pills: Once a week: one output, end to end

lines: Keeping a human in the loop doesn't mean a human reading every page.
It means a human deciding, in advance, what cannot be true if this is going well, and then building the thing that says so.

pills: Decide in advance what can't be true

lines: Four sentences.
Nothing came out.
Everything got through.
Something's missing.
It cost too much.
Write those down for your own team before you set it running, and then, honestly, stop watching it.
